newsitem.title: POLAND: Solidarity chief suggests general strike unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Solidarity chief suggests general strike unlikely.

text.p: Solidarity leader Marian Krzaklewski, whose union has launched a wave of protests against the collapse of the Gdansk Shipyard, said on Thursday the best protest against Poland's ruling ex-communists would be their election defeat later this year.

The union on Wednesday launched nationwide protests to halt the final collapse of the bankrupt shipyard and, after police forcibly ousted workers occupying three ministries in Warsaw, Solidarity chiefs said a general strike was possible.
But before a special Warsaw meeting of the union's national leadership committee Krzaklewski told reporters:
"The best general strike would be elections, in which we vote not for the communist forces, but for Solidarity."

"After democratic elections we will hold the communists to account for all their crimes." said Krzaklewski, who heads the strong right-wing Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance the union has formed to fight the elections due around September.
The union accuses the coalition government dominated by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of being motivated by political spite in letting the yard go under.

SLD Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, who says the government cannot waste more taxpayers' money or press banks to bail out the state-owned yard, was due around midday to present proposals to parliament that might save some Gdansk jobs.

Gdansk newspapers have reported this might involve the more successful Szczecin shipyard subcontracting some work to the Gdansk yard's premises for ships being built for the PZM merchant shipping company.

Solidarity has seized on the final collapse of the yard, where the union arose out of the struggle against communist rule in 1980, to mobilise protests against wider government industrial policy and to mobilise its backers before the polls.

It charges that the government has refused to help out of political spite while Cimoszewicz, whose party reformed as pro-market social democrats after the 1989 fall of communism, has accused the union of exploiting the shipyard's predicament.

The Solidarity national committee meeting was due to decide on some escalation of the national protests -- so far largely consisting of pickets and demonstrations -- especially in light of Wednesday's use of force by police at the Treasury ministry.

"Because of the events in the Treasury ministry, we can expect the national committee to make some very radical decisions on the union protest actions, because this time a blow was struck at basic workers rights," union spokesman Piotr Zak told public radio.
Workers were converging on Warsaw from Solidarity strongholds such as the Silesia mining region for a march on parliament at 3.00 p.m. (1400 GMT) -- an event also due to be repeated on Friday.
Zak said the union, Poland's largest, would listen very carefully to Cimoszewicz before Thursday's march started.
"We will listen very closely. If Premier Cimoszewicz says anything we consider untrue, we will also be protesting against this untruth," he added.

The union has also already announced protests outside provincial government offices around Poland, leading Cimoszewicz to warn in a Wednesday speech that he would not tolerate occupations like those at the Warsaw ministries.

In the Baltic coast city Gdansk, where desperate shipyard workers have held rowdy street demonstrations almost daily for two weeks, about a 1,000 of them marched on SLD offices to shout slogans including "Commies out" and "We want to work."
